Position Responsibilities The Women’s and Gender Studies Department in the Bellarmine College of Liberal Arts at Loyola Marymount University seeks a scholar with a background in social science research and expertise in one or more of the following fields: Black feminism, decolonial or postcolonial studies, environmental justice/queer ecology, or militarism. The applicant would be expected to teach introduction level courses in Women’s and Gender Studies, a course in feminist and queer research methods, as well as an upper division course in the applicant’s area of expertise. Position description The Department of Human Ecology in the College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences at the University of California, Davis is recruiting an Assistant Professor of Community and Regional Development who focuses on community economic development and planning in areas that respond to pressing problems and opportunities (e.g., poverty, inequality, prospects for sustainable economies). Key areas of research could include, but are not limited to, equitable and collaborative economic models, cooperatives, regenerative and climate responsive economies, affordable housing, and climate smart/green technologies. Seeking applicants with applied research and/or professional experience collaborating with diverse government, business, and civic community organizations to maximize public impact of their research. Research focused on domestic and/or global contexts is welcome. This is an academic year (9-month), tenure track Assistant Professor position that includes an appointment in the California Agricultural Experiment Station (AES). Faculty members who hold an AES appointment have a responsibility to conduct research and outreach relevant to the mission of the California AES. Participation in outreach programs and performance of university service are also expected. The appointee is expected to establish a competitively-funded research program (as described above) to address critical or emerging issues that can facilitate or hinder sustainable and equitable economic development and planning in communities. The appointee will be responsible for teaching a typical courseload of three courses per year (usually alternating between 2 and 3 undergraduate plus 1 graduate course every other year). At either level, courses will reflect a combination of core courses and specialized topical courses. Examples include: CRD 1 (The Community), CRD 164 (Community Change Organizations), CRD 156 (Community Economic Development), CRD 172 (Social Inequality: Issues and Innovation), or CRD 171 (Housing and Social Policy) at the undergraduate level; CRD 240 (Theories of Community Development), CRD 245 (Political Economy of Community Development), CRD 250 (Community Development in Practice); GEO 200DN (Methods of Socio-Spatial Analysis in Geography) at the graduate level. Along with teaching, the appointee will engage in mentoring, advising, and curricular development at the undergraduate and graduate levels. Participation in and development of public outreach and/or community engagement programs, and performance of departmental and university service is expected in this position. This position is expected to collaborate with Cooperative Extension specialists and advisors, partners in allied industries or other appropriate policy and public stakeholders. This recruitment is conducted at the assistant rank. The resulting hire will be at the assistant rank, regardless of the proposed appointee's qualifications. Initial review of applications will be conducted using anonymized versions of the Statement of Research Accomplishments and Interests. Applications demonstrating sufficient potential based on this review will be advanced to full review. Availability of Space and Resources Office and laboratory

The outreach component of this position centers on technical consultation and collaboration with management partners and agencies for stock assessment model development and harvest policy evaluation. The position start date is anticipated to be January 2027. Competitive applicants will have experience in quantitative fisheries stock assessment and harvest simulation modeling. Statistical catch-at-age (SCAA) models are used widely throughout the Great Lakes for management purposes, including setting recommended harvest levels for important commercial and recreational fisheries (e.g., lake trout, lake whitefish, walleye) and for determining appropriate stock levels to maintain predator-prey balance in Lakes Michigan and Ontario. The primary responsibility of this position is to develop educational materials (printed materials, in-person and online short courses) on introduction to RTMB, fish population dynamics, stock assessment methodology, and harvest policy methodology to ensure Great Lakes assessment biologists are able to maintain assessment models for management purposes. The hired scientist will work alongside other QFC stock assessment scientists in this curriculum development effort. Other responsibilities of this position will include modernizing SCAA assessment models and evaluating sustainable harvest policies for key managed species. Applied work will include involvement with the bi-nationally managed Lake Erie walleye and yellow perch fisheries, valued at more than $1 billion USD/yr and which presently are the only Marine Stewardship Council certified fisheries in the Great Lakes, in close collaboration with the Lake Erie Committee (LEC), Standing Technical Committee (STC), Lake Erie Walleye Task Group (WTG) and the Yellow Perch Task Group (YPTG). This position offers meaningful research opportunities, including exploration of state-space modeling frameworks, hierarchical approaches to stock assessment, and simulation-based evaluation of harvest policies. This researcher will join an engaged team of fisheries scientists working at the Quantitative Fisheries Center tasked with improving fishery stock assessments throughout the Great Lakes.
